profiles.meeting_scenario: At a 900-bed academic medical center, a 30-minute coordination meeting is being held to align the critical care practice redesign workstream with the EHR build workstream before a 3-week pilot of a standardized change-of-shift handoff in the Medical ICU (MICU) and Surgical ICU (SICU). The pilot is scheduled to start on July 15 and is meant to support an evidence-based handoff approach while fitting existing critical care workflows. The agenda is to confirm what content will appear in the handoff tool, what the training packet should reference, which patients and shifts are included in the pilot, how adoption will be tracked, and who owns last-minute updates. The expected outcome is apparent alignment on the pilot package, training dependencies, and monitoring plan so each workstream can proceed without further escalation.

members.name: Leah Benton
members.expertise: ICU nursing workflow, evidence-based practice implementation, bedside handoff standardization, staff education
members.background: Leah spent 11 years as a bedside nurse in mixed medical-surgical critical care and now leads nursing practice changes across the MICU and SICU, including the current handoff standardization pilot.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to feel practical to bedside nurses and fears that if the rollout looks like an IT project rather than a nursing practice change, charge nurses and preceptors will quietly resist it.
hidden_assumptions: A 'standardized handoff template' is primarily the verbal sequence and bedside safety check nurses are taught to perform, with the EHR only serving as a support.
The 'current handoff form' means the paper report sheet and unit-specific notes nurses actually carry during shift change, because that is what shapes real practice.
When the pilot is said to cover MICU and SICU, it includes all patients handed off by those nurses, including overflow and boarded patients physically assigned to those teams.
A handoff is 'complete' when the standardized verbal structure is used and the bedside line-drain-airway check occurs, even if documentation is minimal.
If something is 'ready for pilot,' the content is stable enough that educators can train to it without expecting material changes during the pilot window.

members.name: Arjun Patel
members.expertise: EHR workflow configuration, nursing documentation tools, operational reporting, implementation coordination
members.background: Arjun is a former step-down RN who moved into informatics and now manages nursing documentation builds, reporting logic, and release coordination for inpatient workflows.
members.private_state: He wants to keep the build inside the existing release package and avoid custom exceptions that would create support burden or delay promotion to production.
hidden_assumptions: A 'standardized handoff template' is the shared EHR handoff navigator layout and prepopulated data view that nurses open during report.
The 'current handoff form' refers to the existing printed EHR shift summary, since that is the only artifact his team can map and revise consistently.
When the pilot is said to cover MICU and SICU, the population is defined by the patient location codes tied to those units in Epic reporting tables.
A handoff is 'complete' when the nurse opens the handoff navigator and signs the handoff checklist event that can be counted in the audit report.
If something is 'ready for pilot,' it means the build is in TEST/UAT and available for validation, even if wording or field order may still change before production.

misalignment_points.topic: What the 'standardized handoff template' actually is
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss getting the 'standardized handoff template' ready for the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Leah means the nurse-facing practice standard: a fixed verbal sequence, bedside safety check, and agreed content order that educators will teach.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Arjun means the EHR handoff navigator and its fields, tabs, and auto-pulled data elements that will be available during report.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In a coordination meeting, 'template' naturally sounds like a shared artifact bridging practice and IT, so each person hears the term as inclusive of their own domain and does not see a reason to separate the concept.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'current handoff form' is being cleaned up
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to pulling key items from the 'current handoff form' so nurses are not starting from scratch.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Leah is thinking of the unofficial paper brain sheets used by experienced ICU nurses, especially the handwritten prompts for drips, lines, and contingency plans.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Arjun is thinking of the existing EHR shift summary printout that already pulls labs, code status, isolation flags, and active orders.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Each unit informally uses both artifacts, and staff often talk about them interchangeably as the handoff form, so the reference feels obvious even though they are indexing different objects.

misalignment_points.topic: Who is included when they say the pilot is 'for MICU and SICU'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the pilot will run in MICU and SICU starting July 15.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Leah assumes the pilot covers all shift-to-shift reports performed by MICU and SICU nurses, including ICU patients boarding in PACU and medicine overflow patients occupying ICU beds under critical care nursing staff.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Arjun assumes the pilot only applies to patients whose location code at handoff time is MICU or SICU, because that is how the tool exposure and audit logic are configured.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Unit names are a natural shorthand in hospital operations, and both speakers are used to saying 'MICU/SICU pilot' without explicitly unpacking whether that means staff-based scope or location-based scope.

misalignment_points.topic: What will count as 'completion' or 'adoption' in the first two weeks
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both want to review 'completion rates' and 'adoption' after the first two weeks of the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Leah means adoption demonstrated through educator observation that nurses followed the standardized verbal sequence and performed the bedside safety check during sampled shift changes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Arjun means completion measured by EHR events such as opening the navigator and documenting the handoff checklist, producing a dashboard percentage.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both criteria sound like reasonable operationalizations of the same goal, and because pilot evaluation is not the headline agenda item, the phrase 'completion rate' slips by as if it were self-evident.

For me, the standardized handoff template is the verbal sequence and bedside safety check the educators will teach, with the chart just backing that up. And when we say MICU and SICU, I mean every report those nurses are giving on July 15, including overflow and boarded patients, because that's what staff will experience as the pilot.
